scenes.title: Watch the whole journey first

beats.text: Consider a cyclist riding along a flat road. She is moving, so she has energy of motion... kinetic energy.
Now the road climbs a hill. She pushes hard on the pedals and, as she climbs, she actually gets faster.
At the top she is higher than before... and moving faster than before. Two things changed at once.
Her height went up, so her gravitational potential energy went up. Her speed went up, so her kinetic energy went up too. Today we measure both.

scenes.title: Kinetic energy: the energy of motion

beats.text: Start with a moving car. Mass fifteen hundred kilograms, travelling at twenty metres per second.
Kinetic energy equals a half, times mass, times speed squared.
A half, times fifteen hundred, times twenty squared.
That is three hundred thousand joules. Three hundred kilojoules.
Kinetic energy is a scalar. It has size but no direction, and it can never be negative. A parked car has none at all.
Because the speed is squared, doubling the speed gives four times the kinetic energy. Speed matters a lot.

scenes.title: The change in kinetic energy

beats.text: When the speed changes from u to v, the kinetic energy changes. The change is final minus initial.
beats.ink: Δ K E = ½ m v² − ½ m u²

beats.text: Take out the half m. The change in kinetic energy is a half m, times v squared minus u squared.
beats.ink: Δ K E = ½ m (v² − u²)

beats.text: Careful: it is the difference of the squares, not the square of the difference. Square each speed first, then subtract.
If the object slows down, v is less than u, and the change is negative: kinetic energy was lost.

scenes.title: Gravitational potential energy: the energy of height

beats.text: Lift a box slowly to a height h above the floor. The force needed is its weight, m g, and it moves through h.
Gravitational potential energy equals m g h: weight times vertical height above the level you chose.
beats.ink: G P E = m g h

beats.text: You choose the level where the potential energy is zero, usually the ground. Height is measured from there.
Moving up gains potential energy... moving down loses it. And a moving object at a height has both kinds at once, like our cyclist.

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The full question. A cyclist and her bicycle together have mass m, unknown. On the flat, she rides at four metres per second.
She climbs a hill three metres high, and reaches the top at eight metres per second. Her kinetic energy increased by two point four kilojoules.
Take g as ten. Find the total mass, and the gain in gravitational potential energy.
Before we start: which formula has the unknown mass in it, with everything else known? Take a moment.

scenes.text: full question. A cyclist and her bicycle together have mass m, unknown. On the flat, she rides at four metres per second. She climbs a hill three metres high, and reaches the top at eight metres per second. A kinetic energy increased by 2 .4 kJ. Take GS10. Find the total mass and the gain in gravitational potential energy. Before we start, which formula has the unknown mass in it with everything else known? Take a moment.

scenes.title: First, find the mass

beats.text: The change in kinetic energy is a half m, times v squared minus u squared.
beats.ink: Δ K E = ½ m (v² − u²)

beats.text: Two point four kilojoules is two thousand four hundred joules. Convert before you substitute.
So two thousand four hundred equals a half m, times eight squared minus four squared.
Eight squared is sixty-four, four squared is sixteen. Sixty-four minus sixteen is forty-eight.
Half of forty-eight is twenty-four. So two thousand four hundred equals twenty-four m.
Divide by twenty-four. The mass is one hundred kilograms.

scenes.title: Then, the gain in potential energy

beats.text: Gain in gravitational potential energy is m g, times the gain in height.
beats.ink: Δ G P E = m g Δ h

beats.text: One hundred, times ten, times three.
Three thousand joules. Three kilojoules gained.
So at the top she has three thousand more joules of potential energy, and two thousand four hundred more joules of kinetic energy. Both, at the same time.

scenes.title: What would change on the way down?

beats.text: What if she now rolls back down the same three metres? The height change is minus three, so the change in potential energy is one hundred, times ten, times minus three: minus three thousand joules. A loss.
